utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear at this trial with my learned friends, Mrs Teresa McHenry, Mr Giuliano Turone and our case manager and legal assistant, Miss Elles van Dusschoten. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do we have the appearances for the defence, please, with the first counsel for the first defendant? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Edina Residovic, defence counsel for the accused, Zejnil Delalic, with co-counsel, Professor O'Sullivan and Ekrem Galijatovic, attorney. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Counsel for the second defendant? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney from Belgrade, with my co-counsel, Mira Tapuskovic, also attorney from Belgrade. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May we have the appearances for the third defendant? MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, with co-counsel, Mr Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Finally, but not the least, may we have the appearances for the fourth defendant? MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Attorney Mustafa Brackovic from Sarajevo with co-counsel Miss Cynthia McMurrey, attorney from the United States, from Houston. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This morning, we have the opening speech by counsel for the second defendant, Tapuskovic. Can we hear you, Mr Tapuskovic, your opening speech? Opening statement by MR TAPUSKOVIC MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour of the Trial Chamber of the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague. I wish to greet you on my behalf and on behalf of my co-counsel, and what I am about to present in the next minutes is something that is a product of our joint effort and we will try to present the issues before you today. I had requested a little time yesterday, and I want to thank you for giving me this extra time. I am mentioning this because I wanted to double check on certain things, including the order of witnesses, and this is the new order of witnesses which was provided to us yesterday, and it included some new names, because in late December, it had been presented in a different way. There were fewer witnesses then, and there was very little time for me to see of what significance this may be for my opening statement, which I am about to present before you, and I believe that what I have gotten from the prosecution does not interfere with what I have to say today, but I had not been sure, but having been given enough time from you, I was able to double-check. In the former Yugoslavia, if we look at the history and the sociological issues, we can go on for a very long time. However, I am defending one single individual, and I will address the evidence and also his personal state in the circumstances in which he found himself and for which he has been charged in the indictment before you. I may be interested only in the defence of Mr Mucic. I never lent on the other accused, and so I am only focusing on the personal story of Mr Mucic, but the obvious facts I cannot bring into question, because I never defended in different situations without not taking into account the facts which I had to grapple. Some of the most general things that are here before you, and will be in the coming months, I would like to see presented as fast as possible, because it is our interest, and also that of the defendant himself, who has been in detention, that this trial be as expeditious as possible. In the beginning, I will say a few things. I have been an attorney for thirty years. I do not know how many final arguments I have given, but this is the first time that I am giving an opening statement. This is the first time, as I say, that I am giving an opening statement, and I think that I am the first attorney from the former Yugoslavia who is going to give it. We had a different case in the Erdemovic case, because he had admitted his guilt, and so there was no opening statement there, and I believe that my colleague will have an easier job of it later, when it comes their turn. Whether this opening statement is going to be in the spirit of the common law, because I have never given one before, and I probably would not have done so had it not been this case here in The Hague, and thanks to my colleagues from the US and Canada, when I spoke to them about how I should proceed, they said that this is indeed in the spirit of what a defence attorney is supposed to do, and I want to thank them for it. I also have heard Mr Ostberg, and I can see that my opening statement also is going along the lines of what he has said. What is my purpose of this opening statement? I would like to assist you to be able to enter into the issues as soon as possible, and to start paying attention to the issues that will be presented through the witness statements and the written documents presented by the prosecution, and also through the ability that you have to question witnesses yourselves, and even present certain evidence, and this is where the difference is between the common law legal system, because some of the authority that you have also is not part of that system either. In my pre-trial brief, I have given a framework for my theory of defence, and now I would first like to point to the evidence offered by the prosecution, which also corroborates my theory, which was presented in my pre-trial brief. So, in my opening statement, I will not present any of the evidence that I may be presenting here, before this chamber, but I will only point to all the exculpatory evidence that the prosecution has had in its possession, with respect to Mr Mucic, and how it completely disregarded it. This is why I am giving this opening statement now, right after the Prosecutor's opening statement, and not waiting for the prosecution case in chief to be completed. This is a strategy, and I have to point this out right away. Mr Mucic, the defendant, has been waiting a full year for this trial to start. On March 18th, it will be one full year since he has been detained. My colleague, McHenry, at one of the status conferences, mentioned a case, I do not know where it was, but she said that this was not a long period of time, and that we had not been waiting long, because somewhere there was a case where people waited seven years for the start of a trial. Such comparisons in cases -- and I am not talking about this case; I am talking about the protection of human rights -- detained persons have some basic rights, and then, again, I can call on Article 12 of the Statute of this Tribunal, where it calls for a fair, but also an expeditious trial. If we have trials going on for several years here, these trials will not fulfil their purpose, and they will affect adversely people who are waiting in detention to be tried. I know what a single day in a prison means, and so I feel obliged to mention this before this chamber. In the transcripts from the previous status conference, you know that the trial had been set for October 1st 1996. You asked me how much time I needed for my opening statement presentation if I had been preparing it for one year. I have not been preparing it a full year. I only needed one month, because I saw the evidence that the prosecution had at the time of the indictment, and I spent most of that time just verifying certain things that the accused offered themselves, and, when I first came here, I already had what I am talking about today, and so I was able to address all these issues, even in October, and I would not have needed more than fifteen days, indeed. Then the trial had been set for 12th December, 28th January and then finally we reached this day, practically a full year from the moment when he was detained, and when, in Vienna, he was told to come here as soon as possible, and he agreed to that, because he believed that his trial was going to start very soon. In the meantime -- and this is something I need to mention too -- he found a very inappropriate way to express his dissatisfaction with this. He went on a hunger strike, and I was cautioned by the Tribunal as if I had inspired him to that. I know that this was absurd, but it was the only way that he knew how to express his dissatisfaction, and this is why I am using this opportunity to give this opening statement now, but also in order for you to be able to start understanding the issues right away, and obviously it is up to me to try to present it as well as I can. So here we are at the beginning of this trial. This opening statement could maybe be more convincing after the presentation of the prosecution case, but I decided to do it now, and it was not easy. You know that the Rules of the evidence are not complete, and you invited us to participate in overcoming the issues, and both myself and my co-counsel will act in this spirit of that. In many ways, we have not been in an equal position with respect to the prosecution. We only got the full conditions for work a few days ago, but I am not going to dwell on it. If you look around, we have the state of the art computer technology, but what I am looking for, I just need a little space to jot things down. This is not what I am used to, and I do not have it here, but trust me, I would like that the justice before this Tribunal be at the level of the computer equipment that we have. Also, if you allow me, I will have a digression. Mr Wladimiroff, the defence attorney of Mr Tadic, he gave an interview to the only Yugoslav newspaper that has been following the trial. I think the journalist from there may be present here. It is the Nasa Borba. He said this, and I quote: "People in authority in the former Yugoslavia have a very strange attitude towards the truth, towards the possibility that people speak freely what they know, and what they think. This is one of the reasons why I truly feel sorry for my colleagues from the former Yugoslavia who will be involved in future cases. I can say whatever I want, but they have problems, because back at home they will be asked, 'Why did you say that?'." Is that really true? We could turn this around. Even if you were able to say everything, by not knowing the language of the accused, is it possible to have a full communication with him to find all the relevant information, and can all the exculpatory elements in the defence be known without knowing the environment in which these events took place and the mentality of people that took part in them? Mr Wladimiroff may have a point. You may know the position of my colleague, Galijatovic, who, at one of the status conferences, in the transcript I was given a lot of compliments there, but then it was said that for people in Sarajevo, it is an act of provocation to have an attorney from Serbia that is from Yugoslavia, from Belgrade, who is defending one of the accused here. But why not, I am asking you? Have we not had a peace agreement signed? Must we not continue to communicate about the events that took place in that region? Do we need not provide services in hospitals as well as in courtrooms? That is just one of the aspects. Another aspect is I also had very unpleasant moments in Belgrade for my own extended family. Some of them said that they would change their names if I came to The Hague. How can I, an ethnic Serb, defend an ethnic Croat? That is absurd, when I gave my oath, as an attorney, I never dreamt that this time would come that, if somebody approached me and asked me to defend them, that I first asked him, "You are a Croat, so if you are a Croat I cannot defend you because I am a Serb". But we will continue to live there. There will be traffic accidents. People will have to be defended. So I do not want to belabour that point. Then the press, the media. They attacked me. They said, "Tapuskovic is defending the beast of Celebici". You see the indictment, you saw what he is charged with. I had a colleague, a judge on the Supreme Court in Serbia, and he said, "You will just ruin your own career, you will get your own Serb now". I am not sure if that is what Mr Wladimiroff had in mind. He may have had something else in mind. There is belief back in the past in Yugoslavia we could never speak freely, we could never think freely, but we will see here in this country whether we can say things openly, but I can tell you at all times in that region there were people who dared speak the truth, even at the price of their freedom or life, even among lawyers. This is what I felt I needed to say, and in the following months, we will address the war in the former Yugoslavia, the victims that it produced, in one of the places where horrible things went on. However we call this war, it was a senseless and unnecessary suffering of people. There are people who are more or less guilty. That whole region in the whole of its history never had 50 years of continuous peace, as they had between 1945 and that war. That is the only period when there was no suffering, and in all these places -- and I can speak of Belgrade, which was not swept into the war, that there is post-Vietnam syndrome present because of the terrible things that had happened in different front lines in that region. Many of us knew about different problems in various areas of that country, and we all believed that a war would not come and I believe all of us present here never believed in it. I will not dwell on the causes and the characteristics of this war, and I probably will not have many questions for the expert witnesses, with that respect, and I will not enter into any polemics with the prosecution on that issue. There is one cause of that war that has not been mentioned by the prosecutor, and that is the basic thing, which is why all of it happened. It was a product of people who were thirsty for power. That reason was not mentioned by the prosecutor, and you may or may not know it is one of the worst motivations, and its name is power. Now they can all sit nicely in their chairs, and we had this tradition of people who, once they got the power, that they would never leave it. They do not care about what is going on, but let us not dwell on that either. I am here to defend Mr Mucic, and I state that, given the abundance of the evidence from the prosecutor's arsenal, had there been more people like Mucic, there had never been the war, and, if it was up to him, there would not be a single victim there, and I will try to demonstrate that, based exclusively on the evidence offered by the prosecution. Among their evidence, you have a statement by Mira Golubovic, and you will hear that. He will be one of the first witnesses here. He said to the investigators of this Tribunal, had there been 20 per cent of the people in Bosnia and he was one of the victims, like Mucic, there would not have been war. Unfortunately, the investigators who were questioning Mucic stopped questioning at that time, stopped at this point, obviously not satisfied with this kind of statement, and also when they were questioning his father, Slavoljub, it is also there. So at this point, we do not have it on the prosecution witness list, but we have it in the witness statements, and he literally said, "He saved my life". I need to depart again from this case and go to something that is linked to this. It is something that the prosecution wants to use in order to control the situation here regarding Mr Mucic. There is something in the case file of Mr Mucic that makes all these charges absurd, and I have been pointing to this in the various status conferences, and we debated this, and I was expounding my position, and I even filed a motion, and I think it was an awkward motion, because I asked something of the Trial Chamber, even though it actually should have been directed to the prosecution. There is a document from Konjic, and it is in possession of the prosecution, and I am sure they will use it, but you will see in what way. There is a verdict sentencing Mucic to 15 years in prison. He was convicted of Esad Bubalo in abstentia. He was sentenced to that. In the verdict, this murder took place on 27th June 1992, and the victim was Esad Bubalo. Mucic was convicted not for committing the murder, and the point is that it is the same here, because he was also sentenced for something that he had not done there, but that he had ordered it, and that he was also the camp commander at that time. In other words, that murder coincides with the time period from this indictment. Also the place of the time is the same, and Bubalo was a prisoner. He was the only ethnic Muslim who was a prisoner in this camp, and I need to point this out to the Trial Chamber, and I think that it should be part of your very serious consideration, because the prosecution will do everything to convince you that he was a commander, and so that we have nothing to discuss about that case here. As soon as I saw this verdict, as soon as I saw it, without the full case file, and after reviewing the file, it was clear to me that this was nothing but a framer, and these kind of fabrications I have seen a lot in the past. I even wrote a book about it. But there was no cause of death. There were different times of the commission of this murder cited and only a photograph of the grave where he was buried, and the only proof was a statement of a co-defendant, who was also not a direct perpetrator. In August of 1996, I filed a motion pursuant to Rule 9 of the rules of evidence regarding deferral of competence, saying that this was not a common crime, but a crime against humanity. If we have some 50 counts on the indictment, we could have included one more, because at that time the proceeding was not conducted with due diligence, and this case also involves significant factual and legal issues relevant for this proceeding as well. From Mr Ostberg I got a reply that he was a fellow soldier, and it was a common crime, so my motion should be understood properly. It may look paradoxical, but, if you look at it this way, then please note it in that respect, and you will see that the prosecution dwells on this, you will see from their presentation. Mr Ostberg told me that they will not do that, that it was a common crime, and that he was a fellow soldier. The verdict was passed in abstentia, and he said that it was going to be retried, but the case could have come here. Now, we could debate that. We could discuss it, to what extent it would be in the spirit of the Rules of this Tribunal. But, in the files, there is a piece of evidence that the prosecution will use, and I will give you one statement. This is a quote from a statement that will be presented by the prosecution, and I quote: "Look, I was under an impression throughout the trial against me that it was in everyone's interest to prove that Pavo Mucic was responsible only because he was a Croat, and to demonstrate that Mucic ordered the killings of Muslims, and so forth, because this trial took place during the worst conflict between the Muslims and Croats. This has been haunting me all this time", it says in the statement. "I lied with respect to this man. A man can be accused even though he is completely innocent. In other words, it was in the interests of the people who put us on this trial. Please, the entire trial was a matter of a deal. After a lot of persuasion, I finally agreed to tell them what suited them, so that they would reduce the charges against me. Behind all of this, behind the Bubalo murder are some people who are still in the positions of power. For instance, it was easier to blame it all on Pavo Mucic so that in no way I would be at risk for any retaliation. "Pavo Mucic was not the prison commander at that time of Bubalo's murder." This is a quote. The prosecution has it among its evidence material, and I want them to present it to you. That kind of verdict in abstentia against Mucic, based exclusively on a statement at variance with the one that you just heard by the same person, is what the prosecution will try to introduce. The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina have this document, that the commander of the camp was Mr Mucic, even though, in the case file, there is no proof, written proof that he was a camp commander. In other words, he was only sentenced because somebody said that he was a commander. In other words, now we have a verdict, a sentence, treating him as camp commander, a Croat belonging to the HVO, and now he is guilty for everything that went on there. So I need to point to you at this time that I will certainly not agree, when the time comes, that the Bubalo file, which is pretty thick, be presented here as any kind of evidence. Maybe it can. We will see when the time comes. If the entire file is translated, so that you can read it and, as experienced judges, make a decision on it, then we can go and see who fabricated the whole case. I will also need to warn you of another thing. This trial was first conducted in Mostar, before the Croatian Community, Herceg-Bosna, within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then it was stopped, and then that was the end of the case. Once the case was closed, it is over. So the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had filed the case, and I will show you one more thing about how certain cases can be fabricated. Everything I am saying here, I am not talking based on the evidence that I collected. I am only talking about the evidence offered by the prosecution. So I am not making anything up. I am not construing anything. This is all evidence of materials from the prosecution. There is no criminal charge against Pavo Mucic from the Republika Srpska. However, it exists, but it is against another person. How shall we explain that? At the same time on 22nd December 1992, and then again on 12th February 1994, they filed charges for war crimes, but now against Pavo Mucic, and another citizen, I do not know if it was in Bosnia or Croatia, but of Croatian ethnic background, and that refers to the Celebici camp. That is the same matter, that is the same system, that you have just heard, when I quoted that witness statement, and it is not something that I construed. Again, I have to ask this question: why the prosecution does not treat a closed legal case in the same way as the verdict from Konjic. And why did it pursue this event? You will see later when we go to the indictment. Why? I think for now I only request, and you will see more when we start hearing the evidence, I do not know if the prosecution is going to change their position. Whoever has been questioned by the prosecution in half of their statements, they had to explain these facts: What was with respect to that? When did who become camp commander? But they were not pursuing the event itself, the crime against humanity. Here we can debate forever, and I do not mean just the situation of this trial. When in the world shall we -- I am sorry, maybe I am belabouring this point. Maybe you do not have enough will to listen to all of this. I think that it is an issue that should be addressed at this time. There are three issues of a more general nature that need to be taken into account here: the first issue is what are the witnesses that may be of interest to the Pavo Mucic defence, only those? I think that they are appropriate witnesses for his situation, and again I remind you, what I am addressing here is his situation, and his position here. So it is the people who were working in the camp, and he would like nothing more than to bring all those whom he helped during their stay in Celebici. He is not interested in any other witness from Sarajevo, or from Zagreb, who was in some position of authority, but never set a foot in that camp. So he is interested in that, and I am interested in these witnesses, and he is not afraid to face all witnesses and discuss all the issues before this chamber. We have a situation which is not allowed in many other prisons in the world. Pavo Mucic is in a position to speak to some of the persons who are not in the prosecution list on the telephone, and he never requested anything of them, and we never asked anything from anybody, had we been given an opportunity to contact the witnesses and just request of them to say everything that they know, without any persuasion. Yesterday, we talked about that, and there is this presumption that the defence would sort of exercise pressure, but we are only interested in one thing: to talk to them, to gain an impression about these persons, and to maybe request them not to be shy and to speak everything that they know, but speak truthfully. But we have not been given this opportunity, and we find that discriminatory to think that we would be blackmailing them, or we would be pressuring them into this or that. We think that that position is wrong, the position taken yesterday, that we cannot have any contact with witnesses, and, after these telephone conversations that Mr Mucic had with people who lived in Germany and Serbia and Bosnia, this is what he got as a typical answer. They said, "Pavo, but you do not need this, where are you calling from?" And they were surprised when they found out he was in jail, and they said, "But please do not, I am in an awkward position". So you will hear witnesses who are going to testify before you who said of one of the persons in this camp, "Several years later he told the story that he will keep Pavo Mucic's photograph next to his patron saint". When we called him, because he read something about how Mucic was setting people on fire, he said, "No, I will not do it". So you have to take that into account as well, that people will come here with preconceptions, and it is something that is very much part of this trial, and this will be the end of my introductory part of my statement. I would now request five minutes to prepare for the next portion of my statement. I do not know whether the translating unit will be able to translate this, but people were saying that hearsay it was that Pavo Mucic was taking money in order to release people, but nobody actually said -- the prosecution never actually said who those people are by name, or what amounts of money they brought, he took. Even the Sarajevo press said he released 200 to 300 people and that he collected money for that. But I will only quote two witnesses, Mira Golubovic and Grozdana Cecez, and I think she will be testifying in the next couple of days. Is she a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No. Excuse me, your Honour, excuse me for interrupting. She is not protected, but there are some other witnesses who we have not yet filed for protection yet, but we believe may want it, so we would just ask counsel to please not speak of the names of possible witnesses, until they come and we know for sure whether or not they request protection. Sorry for the interruption. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, no problem. I will quote other witnesses, because I know that they are protected, but I am sorry if I mentioned this name, because that name was not among the protected ones. So please, my apologies. It is not my point to tell of name and last name of witness F. There will be witness F in the next few days coming, and you will hear from him, your Honours, that Pavo received money, that she received money from Pavo, that Pavo helped her in order to cross to the Serb territory. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, I thought you were making an opening speech. Try to keep it as an opening speech, and let us not get into this. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, it is an opening statement. Again, I already said that everything that I am going to address is only for the benefit of your entering into the case as soon as possible, but I do not think that I can be forbidden presentation of certain things in order to demonstrate the prosecutor's evidence as something that could have been used in a very different way. If I cannot do that, then my opening statement does not make much sense. I am not saying anything that has not been offered by the prosecution already. So that is the purpose of my opening statement at this time. Can I have a five minute break, please, at this point? I only need about five minutes, I am a bit exhausted. I would like to -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, I have the intention of not breaking until you conclude. When you conclude your opening speech, we will break for lunch. So you can carry on. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): I can certainly carry on, like Mr Ostberg did yesterday, but I must admit that I will proceed in the manner I have started, because that was allowed to the prosecution, and I have already said that I will not talk about evidence that I may intend to present, but I am doing this because my aim is for you to be familiarised with these problems from the outset, so that it may be easier to accomplish your task, and I have read a little, and I know from before that such an opening statement has this very purpose, and, following trials in American courtrooms, I remember that statements were always in this sense. From tomorrow such and such will happen, and that is what I wanted to do, but I appeal to you once again, please have a little understanding for our background, that this is the first time that we are involved in a trial of this kind, but I will do my best to respect all the Rules, and I am not going beyond the frameworks of the competence of an opening statement. If you interrupt me, as I go along, then there is probably no purpose in this opening statement. In the indictment, it says that Pavo Mucic was commander of Celebici camp approximately from May 1992 to November 1992. Is such a definition of the time of the beginning of his competencies, the word "approximately" and then "up to November", is that permissible? In my pre-trial brief, I indicated that in its pre-trial brief the prosecution deviated from the indictment. This deviation is such that I may perhaps have asked the prosecution to state in writing whether this is an amendment to the indictment, which is subject to sub-rule 50A of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, where it says that the prosecution may amend an indictment without leave at any time before its confirmation, but thereafter only with leave of the judge. This is an amendment that applies to Pavo Mucic only. In the pre-trial brief of the prosecution, which I hope you have read, on page 5 it says: "Mucic, camp commander, at least from beginning of June." If that is so, then in the indictment, instead of the words "approximately from May 1992", it should have said, "At least from beginning of June of that same year". For a slip of this kind, last year the prosecution was allowed the right to amend the indictment, and this amendment is of a substantive nature. The prosecution may again say that it is a slip, an error. Maybe it is indeed, and, when the time comes, I would like the prosecution to tell us something about this. I could have asked for an explanation and a ruling on this request from the court. I did not do that, and I will not, because it is not in Pavo Mucic's interests to have the trial postponed further, and it is very important for us that the trial begin as soon as possible. I am saying all of this because, by such a statement, the indictment itself has been compromised with respect to Mucic, and the events that took place in May 1992. Almost all the detainees reached the camp before May 31st, 1992, and a very small number arrived after that date. To this, we should add another fact, which the prosecution, in its pre-trial brief, mentions for the first time. The prisoners were beaten up by the soldiers who brought them to prison. From the prosecutor's evidence, it emerges that there was not a single person confirming that Mucic was present in bringing the detainees, transporting them to the camp. Nor did he ever participate in their admission to the camp. Why am I mentioning this? Because three of the tragic outcomes described in paragraph 22 of the indictment, points 13 and 14, the death of Vujicic, Mrkajic and Gligorevic occurred at the entrance to the camp as a result of such a behaviour of the soldiers on 27th May 1992. This is confirmed by the following witnesses: (redacted) (redated)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am very sorry, but I thought counsel was not going to mention the names of people who may or may not be witnesses, because some of them may or may not later ask for protection or choose not to be witnesses, so I am very sorry for interrupting, but I must ask again that counsel not do that, and that any names of possible witnesses be taken out of the transcript. Thank you. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): I will not mention a single name any longer. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. As I indicated, try to make it an opening speech, and not a detailed criticism. It is an opening speech. Make it as general as you can. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): I was going to add witnesses E and F, because these that I mentioned were not on the protected list. I am trying to be as general as possible, but, in order to present the basic thesis of my defence, and the question of extreme necessity that the defendant was in, and in order to explain, while this is of interest to you, I cannot do that unless I draw attention to certain things. I will not mention a single name of any more witnesses, but I will tell you what can be concluded from the evidence of the prosecution, and how this affects my general position, and that is my position regarding the position of Mr Mucic at the time. How am I going to explain this to you and explain my general theory of defence without indicating again any of the evidence of the prosecution? From this wavering on the part of the prosecution, which may affect the substance of the matter, one may raise the question of the correctness of the indictment at least in relation to Mucic if, at one point, it can be said "approximately May" and then "at least the beginning of June"; is that not something that calls in question the entire indictment? Now, one may ask, in that period, as the prosecution defines it, "at least from the beginning of June until the month of November", what is the basis for charging Mucic? The prosecution feels that he was in a position of -- in a superior position as commander of the camp, and that, as such, he is responsible for all the events in the camp. From the first status conference, I wish to draw attention to the prosecution and the Trial Chamber that I am not denying that Pavo Mucic was named commander of the camp on 27th July 1992, and that there must have been a decision on such an appointment. He has never denied this from the very first statement he made in Vienna to the police and the court, when he did not even know the timeframe of his responsibility as defined by the prosecution, and so that, in his single statement made between 19th and 23rd March 1996 before the investigating Judges of the International Tribunal in The Hague, he is consistent in claiming that he was appointed commander of the camp on 27th July 1992, and I must tell you that not on any of those occasions -- and he has never made any further deposition since then -- not on one occasion was he told that he was being charged for this and that, for this and that act. Nor was he told what is the timeframe for those events. We heard yesterday from my distinguished learned colleague that he made up this date, or, to put it in simpler terms, that he lied. Such consistency on the part of a defendant is possible only if he is repeating the only thing that he can say, and that he knows of nothing else, and even then, in addition to this fact... (Interruption) As I was saying, in all those three statements, in the police, in the court, and the prosecution to this day has not submitted to us a deposition that we asked for. If he made this up, did he make up also what can be found in all those statements, and that is that he helped people? This is not something that I am saying, but the witnesses of the prosecution are saying. Does that mean that Mr Ostberg thinks that, in addition to making up the fact that he had been appointed commander on 27th July, that he is also lying when he is saying that he helped people, and that he wanted to come to The Hague as soon as possible, only to wait for a year before this trial began? All efforts to reach that document on his appointment have been in vain, and you yourself, your Honour, after a status conference, asked from the Ministry of Justice and the general administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they convey the document on the appointment of Pavo Mucic of commander of Celebici. You received from them the following report, which is evidence that will be used by the prosecution, and I quote: "Such a document has not been found, nor is there any information to show that such a document existed." That document will never be found, and no person of authority will ever say that it existed, and, among the prosecution witnesses, there are statements by witnesses who claim that such a document must have been signed by at least several people, and that is why that document will not appear before this court, but there is no doubt that such a document exists. I must raise a question here: is it possible to operate and perform the functions of commander under conditions of war of a camp of this kind without a clear decision on authorisations and duties? It is not possible to come to such a post without an appropriate decision. Such a person must have clear competencies and duties defined for him. There are no greater competencies than having authority over people in prison, and I am watching here three people bring him into the courtroom. Such things cannot be done without somebody being authorised to do it, and it is, therefore, quite logical that Pavo Mucic could not have had any authority if such authority had not been assigned to him. How is the prosecution dealing with this problem? It simply says, without any supporting evidence, he was camp commander, on the basis of what? Only on the basis of vague statements by witnesses that he was the commander, in the way in which the witnesses put it; they are their impressions and their own unreliable assessments. Anyway, you yourself, you will be able to hear from them in person what they say, and how -- on the basis of what they claim that he was commander. At the same time, these witnesses do not say that Mucic ever addressed them, or gave them any orders or passed any decision in relation to him, or anyone else, in that period up to 27th July, and that is why the prosecution is using the Bubalo case, and which I insisted on a little bit and tired yourself and myself with it. The prosecution is not interested in that case, because of the tragic death of that individual, but simply in order to use such a frame-up as proof that he was commander of the camp, because, in the sentence it says "Pavo Mucic, member of HVO, commander of Celebici", without again saying anything else, except this oral allegation that he was camp commander. Not only is there no decision on appointment among the prosecutor's evidence, but there is not a single decision or order signed by Pavo Mucic before 27th July 1992. There is not a single detainee who said that Pavo Mucic ordered anything in that period preceding 27th July 1992. There is not a single order of any of his superiors, until 27th July, regarding his duties. There is not a single decision on the release of prisoners with his signature. We have witness D. Finally, I managed to do as the prosecution request -- who said that Pavo Mucic had no authority to -- that he had no authority to sign documents on the release of prisoners in that period. What kind of a camp commander would he be if he has no such authority, and who still very conscientiously does this after 27th July? Was there ever such a commander anywhere? Let the prosecution provide us with a single document testifying to his command responsibilities, be it an order or a decision that he took before 27th July 1992, so that we can then discuss the problem as a whole. It cannot find such a document, because it does not exist. Nor will it ever be found. That is evidence that he signed or ordered anything before 27th July. I am sure that the prosecution will not be able to find it. If it does, then we can discuss any solution regarding command responsibility of Pavo Mucic before 27th July. After 27th July, there is an enormous amount of such evidence in the prosecution file. There are release papers for prisoners, signed by him, but before 27th not a single one. There are witnesses testifying that he released entire groups of people with discharge papers. There is a tape of film recording Pavo driving twelve people with his van to their homes, and leaving them there in the period after 27th July -- I do not remember the exact date, but we will see it on the film -- there are witnesses saying that, in that period of time, he recategorised the prisoners. This means really releasing the prisoners. So he is transferred from the first category to the last category, upon which he is immediately released. There is plenty of evidence in that sense. Then again, there is testimony of a witness, without mentioning any names -- you will be hearing him here -- he is among the prosecutor's witnesses, who said on 20th August 1992, Pavo interrogated him. "I was together with another possible witness", who is not on the prosecutor's list, "who was called up for interrogation before me. There is evidence that the prosecution used to show that there was an order for Mucic to hand over his duties between 15th and 18th November. How, then, could he have taken up his duties without an order if a written order was required for him to hand over his duties? My colleague, Brackovic, said at one point in public here it is easy for Mucic's defence when the most important thing is whether there is a decision on appointment dating before 27th July. It is an important question, particularly in the light of Pavo's depositions from Vienna to this point, because, if he was appointed camp commander on 27th July, as he claims, then not only has he nothing to do with events from May, but he has nothing to do with all the events that occurred up to his appointment on 27th July 1992, on condition that all the charges are proven here, so that, according to command responsibility, it would be superfluous to enter into anything prior to 27th July, at least as far as Mr Pavo Mucic is concerned. Of course, a defence that would insist on this alone would be out of place, because, in that time, after 27th July, according to the indictment, certain acts and omissions occurred, described as "grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, which are punishable according to the Statute of the Tribunal". This is only the introductory segment of the defence, and I am yet to explain why I consider this not to be decisive, and that there are other legal elements which can also exclude the responsibility of the accused for the entire period covered by the indictment. Therefore, this defence is not based exclusively on the problem of the appointment of Pavo Mucic as camp commander, because, if that were so, then we would not have much to do here, because he certainly was commander for a certain period of time. Then we could have long ago separated the trial of Mucic and dealt with it very quickly, if that was the only thing of importance. The next issue has to do with the legal point, which is, in my view, indubitable, in spite of the fact that colleagues defending other defendants have a different view. The detainees in the Celebici camp were protected persons according to the Geneva Conventions, and the accused were duty bound to respect the law and customs of war, including the General Article of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Of course, one might spend months discussing the characteristics of the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Was it an international armed conflict? Did it have characteristics of different conflicts, and believe me it did, although it was a combination of all these things, but I will not dispute these matters. I will not dwell on them at length, because, as I said, I agree that the detainees were protected persons. It is a fact, it is a fact, though I am not disputing this characteristic, nor the competence of this Tribunal, but it is a fact that, in many places, not only in Celebici, but in other places, which are still within the control of Republika Srpska, yesterday's neighbours and friends, suddenly -- it is very difficult to understand this, and this is something you must try to grasp, overnight, or within a week -- one becomes a prisoner, and another one becomes a guard. That is a fact that cannot be denied by anyone. I cannot present Mucic's defence here without going into these problems, and without asking you to bear this phenomenon in mind all the time. We can find all kinds of statutory rules and deal with this case here if our only concern will be the question of his post as camp commander. There was a war, and one might say that it had the characteristics of all kinds of conflicts, to a greater or lesser extent, and that is enough reason for us to discuss it. It was, as I have already said, one of the most senseless wars in the history of civilisation. Military doctrine hardly knows of any such wars in the past. I will not tire you with this now, and particularly not during the proceedings themselves. I will not go into these things. I will just focus on facts linked to my client, and, regardless of all of that, in the name of the defence of humanity, the moment somebody is captured, or disarmed, especially if he is a civilian, whether he was a civilian or not, whether he was an armed person or not, we will go into this, but in my view, that is not essential, not just in this case, but in any other case. It is quite immaterial. He must have been protected. No one has the right. Once I am arrested to be beaten, our civilisation knows what the punishment is for a murderer. All of you yesterday, the day before, you have heard and seen on TV these past few days the picture of the young Albanian who was tied to a pole and at one point you just see a big boot hitting his face. The question now is whether that person will ever be punished by national courts, and whether anyone will try to find out who he was, but the moment that man was tied to the pole, he must be protected. If the national court does not protect him, somebody must protect him, and one day this must be settled on an international level. I am talking now about something that has nothing to do with this, but the Geneva Conventions, if they intend to protect humanity, then these things have to be covered. I am not -- what I am trying to say is that I cannot deny that these persons were protected. Otherwise what would my role be here, if I were not to admit this and recognise this? That is not only my personal position; it is my profound conviction. I apologise, I really do think that this is all material to the problem that we are discussing, and I am sorry that, after almost an hour and a half, I am coming to the counts in the indictment. I will try to limit these remarks within the half hour left to me. As I am making the opening statement, I am referring only to the prosecutor's evidence, and only to matters related to Mucic's defence, but regarding Mucic and his responsibility in the way that I intend to present my case, it seems to me that we can talk about it only, and that is why I wanted to make these references in the opening statement, when all this has been proven in relation to any of the victims, and only then can we know, can we find out what he knew, or might have known, as the prosecution says. Those are the legal matters that we must focus on here, because, if I was able to influence the prosecution in any way, then I would proceed on the evidence proposed by the prosecution for the beginning, and you will be hearing tomorrow, the day after already, that one witness says that he saw Mucic only once, and another witness will tell you, this other witness also in a couple of days when he addresses you here, that Mucic one day, when he saw some women there, said, "They beat you up and brought you here", and he put them in his van and took them home. Among them was a 13 year old girl, a 13 year old, the same age as his daughter at the time, and let me tell you what he told me. If he had saved that little girl alone, then there was meaning to his life. He saved five women that day, and, when he took out these women too, there was a total of seven women that he took out of the camp and took back home. Therefore, from Count 1 to Count 45 of the indictment, the counts have to do with murder, torture, rape, grave suffering, and injuries and inhumane behaviour. The prosecution is not claiming that any one of these acts was committed by Pavo himself directly, personally, and you will see how many witnesses have been interrogated. There is one witness who said something out of 100 of them, and so you will assess this one against the 100, but you have also witnesses who we will be hearing as of tomorrow who say that the guards did not dare beat people in Pavo's presence, or, "I never saw Pavo when prisoners were being beaten", or, "Pavo Mucic defended the prisoners to a certain extent. Nobody was beating when he was present. The beatings started when he left. I was not beaten while I was in Celebici, because Pavo protected me." All the guards hid, concealed from Mucic what they were doing. You will be hearing this from the prosecution witnesses who will be testifying as of tomorrow. Even among the depositions of many other witnesses that are not on the list of the prosecution is there anything that would incriminate Mucic. Therefore, the prosecution defines Mucic's responsibility on the basis that the principal knew or had reason to know that his subordinates would commit such acts or committed them without taking necessary and reasonable steps to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators. Among all the witnesses, there is only one -- it does not matter what his name is -- which the prosecution proposes that we hear who said, "I know the case when my brother, Rajko, was taken out to be beaten. Then Pavo's car passed by and the guards who were beating my brother hid from Pavo, together with my brother". You will hear this witness, and this is also in the evidence that will be presented by the prosecution. So you see there will be some 100 witnesses, but I have in mind primarily those who were in the camp itself, some 50 of them. Not one of them said that they ever could complain about what happened to them as a result of Pavo Mucic's actions. "Pavo asked me", and they would not complain to Pavo. "Pavo told us to inform him if they were being beaten." Then a doctor says that women would not admit they had been raped, even to him, and, when Mucic was in the camp, these things did not happen, or another witness, "I knew Mucic from before. He looked angry, and he asked me who had beaten me up. I was afraid to tell him. I kept silent, and then he said that he would try to find out." Those are also the prosecution witnesses who you will be listening to as of tomorrow. There is not a single guard who said that he ever told Pavo what had been going on. Of course, on condition that we first prove what happened, that this is proven. I apologise, your Honour. If you are tired, I am not tired, I can go on, if you agree. Now to sort of blow this up a little, if we have one statement against 100, then we have reasonable doubt in all the issues that we are discussing here, because only in that way can we discover the truth of a person's guilt. We should not forget that in the camp, according to the indictment, there were 500 detainees, and here I think that about only 10 per cent were questioned, and Pavo Mucic is not afraid of truth, not afraid for himself, even if all 500 of them came here and told how he behaved towards them. So that was the problem of his knowledge, what he knew. Now we have the issue of what he could have known, and that is something that will be a part of this trial as well, and here we have to assess what was the condition of the prisoners, of several hundred prisoners. According to their own statements, only a few had not been beaten at the moment of entering the camp, and this is also the position of the prosecutor as well. Even in the indictment now the prosecution is trying to also charge Pavo Mucic with some military authorities, but at this point, at this time it is not the relevant point. So all of these people had been beaten, and, again, we also had those three tragic cases at the very entrance gate of the prison. That will be really a matter of your judgment, whether somebody had not followed that directly, and, if nobody told him about these things, was he in position on a day-to-day basis to see whether there was an additional injury on somebody's face, on somebody's body, after they had entered the camp? That is for you to judge. Then, again, is the problem of whether it had happened before or after 27th July, and then it is only in the end that we can determine what Pavo could have known, or should have known of the events going on there. I will present now why he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates would commit such acts or had committed such acts, and had not taken appropriate and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators, because that, in itself, is not enough to ascertain his criminal responsibility, and there is a legal ground to exclude it altogether. There are three kinds of charges here. One is the unlawful confinement of civilians, Count 48, plunder of private property, Count 49, and inhumane conditions, Counts 46 and 47. Pavo Mucic never arrested anybody, never brought anybody to prison, never issued an order to bring somebody to prison. There is not a single piece of evidence, literally, and you can peruse the file offered by the prosecution. There is not a single piece of evidence that confirms that Pavo took part in detaining anybody. Of course, nobody can come to the prison without having been taken into custody, but, if that is proof, then I have no issue with the prosecution here, and the detention of civilians is an active thing. If the prosecution is also claiming that he is responsible for the arrest of the people, that is also something that needs to be proven. Further, there is another truly absurd charge here, and that is that Pavo Mucic was taking property from people. First he arrests them, and then proof of that, and then he takes their valuables. There is not a single witness who had not said that all their belongings, all their valuables had been taken away from them before they entered the camp, and why did we need to charge Pavo Mucic with that? It has nothing to do with him. He never even said that to anyone, to do things like that. It is so logical, based on the witness statements. I was looking through them again. There is not a single witness who does not say that their belongings, their property, had not been taken away from them before entering the camp, but here it is, the charge is still there, against Pavo Mucic, as if he was just taking away jewellery and watches, and, of course, he is dismayed when he reads that, and, if the prosecution is trying to charge him for that, let them present any kind of evidence to that. Regarding inhumane conditions, I will point to one thing. I will not belabour that point. It is a very wide subject, and I am not going to elaborate it during my opening statement. I could spend hours speaking to that point, but I will just address a couple of issues. The conditions in the camp were not a product of a pre-planned activity. They were not part of a decision to create such circumstances to put people in where they would be -- where they would lose their lives. These were all extraordinary circumstances. There was no food for anyone at that time. Houses were sold for a few pieces of bread at that time. In their opening statement, the prosecution says that the situation improved after the ICRC visit, but they only came several times, and that happened in the period after Pavo Mucic took over the post of the camp commander, and why is this situation improving? Is it because of the visit of the ICRC, or maybe was it another thing? We requested, and we offered that in evidence, from defence counsel for Mucic, we sent a letter to the ICRC, and they said this was confidential. Then we sent an additional two letters and asked whether these deliveries that were sent to Celebici actually arrived in Celebici, or were diverted elsewhere. In the prosecution evidence, you will see that Pavo Mucic went to pharmacies armed with weapons to get medicine for the prisoners of the camp. I am not going to be reading these witness names. It is even better, it will save some time. But one of the witnesses says, he says: "For three days we did not receive food, and we were told that the baker was not working, and then Pavo said 'Tell the baker to bring something to eat, or I will release all the prisoners'". This is a witness and he has a name and it is a prosecution witness. I already quoted one who spoke to that. There is an additional witness: "I remember that Pavo was angry because the prisoners were not receiving food for four days. This is pretty much what I wanted to say, and this is within two hours, and this is all I have to say as regards the indictment offered by the prosecution. However, I need to point to one thing. Yes, Pavo was involved in one thing, but what was it? He did everything so that the prisoners could leave the camp as soon as possible, and I will tell you one thing that he told me in confidence. He said, "I did not want to see them be there when the winter comes. There were difficult conditions there in that camp", and again there are a number of witnesses speaking to this. As I said, I mentioned that one witness, he confirmed that Pavo brought seven women out of the prison, and one says, "I want to tell you that Pavo never allowed anyone to be beaten in the camp, and that he saved my life". Said the witness, "He arranged for me and my family to be released. Whenever Pavo was in the camp, there were no serious beatings. This you will hear in a few days. "Pavo helped me and my family. He arranged that I be released from Celebici and that my mother and my father be released from the Musala camp in Konjic. So we will hear from this witness as well, and I think that it is one of the first twenty witnesses. There is another witness: "I saw Pavo only when releasing or transferring prisoners", and from him we will hear how many prisoners it was. I think it is clear what I am trying to say. So from the statements of these six or seven witnesses, and these are prosecution witnesses, witnesses that will be called by the prosecution, the accused, Pavo Mucic, according to their statements, that is before our witnesses take the stand, he released about seven women, about 100 persons, and those are all exculpatory, it is all exculpatory evidence within the legal system, and the framework that I have already set up, and to which I am going to come back in closing. But I have to point to another thing, also brought up by the prosecution. Here we are, the 18th March anniversary is approaching, and the investigation continues. Three days ago, I received two additional pieces of evidence, and one of them is a letter. There is a rule of disclosure, of the exculpatory evidence, and I think that they have a statement by a Serb living, I do not know where, saying that Pavo Mucic rescued a lot of Serbs. Then there is a statement by a different person -- I almost said his name again. For him, the prosecution is only just requesting permission for questioning. He stated that he, meaning Pavo, was there only, meaning Celebici, in order to protect the prisoners to the extent that he could. I do not know if there is any additional exculpatory evidence in the possession of the prosecution, but I am just pointing to the amount of this exculpatory evidence in this case, and whether there is more of that, whether we will be able to find more of that. We have our investigative team; we do not have the team like the prosecution has. We are working on it, and we do not know whether the prosecution has additional things that it has not disclosed to us, and which would further corroborate what I have been speaking to. My basic position is, I think, also becoming clear, and I want to point to it now. That is the mental state of Mucic at the time when he was in the camp. In other words, if there was a state of extreme necessity -- that is a very delicate category in the legal theory, and I am aware of the problems that it involves. I will not repeat -- I will not quote from a recent judgment by this trial, by this Tribunal, but we have been talking about precedents here, and I think that Pavo Mucic's case could be, I do not know that I would have been involved in this kind of work if I did not believe that maybe some day I would also make a contribution, be involved in maybe creating a precedent, because -- and I only have about six or seven sentences to devote to that -- it is clear that Pavo Mucic did not commit any crimes of murder, rape, beating. Looking in the evidence offered by the prosecution, and it is not clear whether we have seen everything because also it should be said that the investigators of the prosecution tried to find that kind of evidence. They were just rushing to find what worked for them, and you will see that, that they will have problems because of that kind of approach of the investigators. So no protected person ever complained to him. He could not have imagined what was going on. So none of his subordinates ever admitted to having done this and that. Provided they had done it, because Mucic himself was in such a position, he never imprisoned anybody, he never took any property away from anyone, he grappled with the problems of daily life there in the war time circumstances. But he did something that is crucial, and, if he were only a commander and he does not dispute that, between 27th July and November, if that is the only thing that we could have dealt with a long time ago, and if that were the only problem, I would have told you a long time ago all this is indisputable, let us just find an appropriate sentence. But that is not the case we have here. If the prosecution in this situation, apart from the process of reaching a judgment on what kind of sentence will be passed here, if we have a trial here where we have a case, the Tadic case, and we have been waiting for four months for the judgment, so if in the theory of the prosecution they also need a judgment to lean on in order to find what would be an appropriate sentence for the superior authority, then what are we waiting for? So now we have the question of what could Pavo Mucic have done, whether he should have engaged in investigations. I will be done in about three minutes. It is 12.00. So should he have investigated, so that he would find out who did what there, and then punish the perpetrators? Or else should he, isolated as he was, try to help people as best he could, release them, drive them home, feed them, help them get to safety? We have been involved in this case now for almost three years. Imagine if Pavo Mucic tried to get involved in things in the same way. He was the only hope of those people who were elderly, who were sick, of whom he thought that they were imprisoned without reason, and he released them in large numbers. So here we need to weigh, provided that the acts from the indictment are proved, what would have been more useful? To investigate and punish his subordinates, you know what an investigation is, he has determined what actually happened, or to try within the limits of his own ability in the war time conditions, and in the situation which was dangerous to both him and his family, to help these people? You will see that a rocket destroyed his house four days after he was appointed a camp commander. So who lobbed -- it is a difficult expression -- but who lobbed this shell into his house at this time? I will not try to second guess what would have happened had he left the camp, or if he acted as quoted in the indictment. So his position is very specific, and we cannot make any comparisons with General Yamashita. You cannot. You cannot base Mucic's judgment on the sentence of General Yamashita. I would be very interested in seeing this. We should do as was done in the Yamashita case. It is obviously your authority to valuate that. I am not going to repeat myself, I have one minute left. This is just to wrap up my argument, and, with the purpose of showing you the way of -- you may follow it or not. I do not pretend to be the smartest one here, but it is in the prosecution evidence that the theory that I have presented here becomes viable. That necessity that I mentioned -- and we will see how it turns out -- that necessity is the result of his moral position which existed even before he came into the post that he occupied, regardless of what and how things happened. There was a real impossibility of a different choice within the parameters of his moral attitude. Would there have been a better solution, given the circumstances, than letting people go home? I wish that the prosecution had also taken that into account, given all the evidence that they had. This is the heart of the indictment. Should we neglect what he actually did, and should we hold him to some standards that were not possible then? At the end of the existence of this camp, some 120 people were left. What happened to 300 or 400 who were saved? If he only saved that one girl, if he only saved 100 people -- and what if we look at those 300 or more people that he saved, and if that is confirmed, what shall we do with that? There were 30 people who remained in the camp, and they went through other prisons and remained in different prisons for an additional two years, and these people went through all kinds of things, and heard all kinds of things, and this is what most of the prosecution evidence is based on. The basis is not the evidence of all the people that were released by Pavo Mucic. Maybe we will finally get the document. Maybe somebody will finally need this document to appear, that he did it because he was ordered to do so. In front of this Tribunal, you had a case, and maybe we will need to use it before this Trial Chamber. This is the end. I am really rushing to finish. This is the Erdemovic case. In that case, he admitted his guilt, but he also mentioned necessity, but he confessed to his guilt, and so this necessity was not addressed very much, because morally and physically he was controlled by other persons, and was forced to do certain things, and what did he do? He killed tens of people. Now what did Pavo do in that similar situation? He saved tens and hundreds of people, and I do not think that it is necessary for me to go any further, and, as unusual as it may seem, I know what extreme necessity is, but, in criminal acts, there are never two identical cases. Each one has to be judged by its own merits, based on the circumstances that were there at the time. We can debate legal theories, but I am only interested in this man, and his situation, and his position. My final word, believe me, Pavo Mucic does not fear any judgments. He already has a fifteen year sentence to which he has been convicted for a crime he never committed, and he is absolutely not afraid of any judgment that you may pass. If Erdemovic got ten years, for what he admitted doing, then what can he expect? Nowhere near the fifteen years that he has already been sentenced to by the Bosnian court, and he is really in a nonsensical situation for something that he absolutely has nothing to do with. I think that we must stop talking about various parties, but, anyway, such a man did not suit any of those parties. He is the only one that diplomatic representatives of his country do not come and visit. The Serb side, to use that term, is not suited by somebody saying that there was a man who assisted the Serbs in that camp. You have seen that the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have condemned him, and sentenced him to fifteen years in abstentia, and I pray to God that one day somebody would look through this file, and see what it is about. As for the Croatian state, or let me be careful of the terms I use, again its interests are not served by talk of the responsibility of a Croat in a Bosnian camp for the Serbs, and thus this man, that all three sides could take pride in, has a fifteen year sentence, and he knows that trials lie ahead for him here too. I feel honoured to be defending such a person. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr Tapuskovic for your marathon opening address. I think we will close for this session and reassemble at 2.30 pm for the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a suggestion. We propose to bring our first witnesses directly after lunch, and that will take some one hour, I think, to present the facilities of the camp, and then we present our witness number 2. So, if we could save one half hour or so off our lunch recess, I would be very grateful. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I wish I understood your suggestion. You mean during the lunch break you could use that time to assemble your facilities? You cannot assemble your facilities within that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I can indeed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose from now, which is about 12.10 to 2.30 pm, I am sure you should be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So 2.00, should it not be fitting for your Honours to commence again? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think 2.30 should be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think we will break off and come back at 2.30 pm. (12.10 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) (2.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon. Before we start the proceedings of this afternoon, we want to dispose of two pending motions. We will start with the first one, which has just come in, and that is the motion to allow the investigators to follow the trial during testimonies of the witnesses. There are a few difficulties with the instruments here. I do not know which of the counsel is getting through. I know the English one is working. The translation in English is working. Which other translation is -- it is working?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mine is not on. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yours is working too? MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I can hear very well. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Which is not working? I think so far everyone on that row is working. How about in the accused section? Is everyone working there? So we can now proceed with the instruments all functioning properly. I was telling you about how we are proceeding this afternoon. Before we start on the proceedings, we have to dispose of two motions which are before us. The first one relates to the motion to allow investigators to follow the trial during the testimonies of the witnesses and the second one has been announced, which has been argued, but which decision we just want to hand down orally, and that is the question of the identity of witnesses sought for defence counsel. I am sure the counsel for the defendants will be interested in the motion to allow investigators to follow the trial during the testimonies of the witnesses. What are the views on it? Let the first defendant answer. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The position of defence counsel of Mr Zejnil Delalic is that the investigators should not be allowed to hear the testimony of other witnesses, the main reason being that the prosecution has proposed several investigators as witnesses before this court, and in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, a witness is not allowed to follow the course of the trial of the proceedings. On the other hand, in conformity with the Rules of the Tribunal, the prosecutor is continuing his investigations, and new evidence may be discovered. Fully representing the principles of a fair trial, I think, while fully representing the ethics of the investigators, they should not be placed in a position to learn of the facts that will be presented before this Trial Chamber. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The second? If there are any other views on the defendants, then we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, attorney Moran for Hazim Delic. Your Honour, it is our view that, if the investigator is going to be a fairly routine witness, for instance, proving up documents, then we have no problem with him following the trial, but, if he is going to be a fact witness, the reason we keep the witnesses from hearing the testimony is so that they do not essentially know what the other witnesses have testified to, and so I think that the court might want to split the investigators into the two different -- actually three different, if there is going to be an investigator who is also an expert, he can probably hear the testimony, or one who is going to be a routine witness proving up a chain of custody, or something like that, as opposed to the third type, which would be a fact witness, and it would be the fact witnesses that we would object to appearing here, of being in the Tribunal, following the evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Any other views? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I think there is no need for me to repeat what Madam Edina Residovic has said. I think this could be admitted on one condition only, and that is, if the investigators of the defence could be in the courtroom all the time, and then we could reach agreement on this together. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Mr Brackovic? MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Esad Landzo's defence counsel would like to support what has been said by attorney Edina Residovic, Thomas Moran. We feel that the presence of investigators during testimony of witnesses would be contrary to the interests of justice, and, in other words, we are opposed to their presence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Mrs McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. It is the case that, with respect to the investigators that the prosecution seeks to be allowed to be present in the public gallery of the courtroom, absolutely none of them are fact witnesses. There is one investigator analyst who may be called as a kind of expert witness with respect to analysis of documents, and then, with respect to all the other potential investigators, the only possible reason that the prosecution is now aware of that they would be called would be for authentication or chain of custody of documents. So they are not at all fact witnesses and therefore, as Mr Moran has correctly pointed out, the purpose of the Rule 90 does not apply to them, and, in fact, given that, as Mrs Residovic has pointed out, there may be other investigation, other issues that come up that need to be followed, it, in fact, would be necessary for the investigators to know something about what is going on, so they can then go do whatever investigative work. But we emphasise that at this point there is no -- we have no belief whatsoever and do not know the circumstances under which it could happen that we would call any of the prosecution investigators, or analysts, as fact witnesses. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, the main argument is that they are, strictly speaking, not ordinary witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Our argument is that, in fact, Rule 90, I believe it is (d), does not really apply. In an excess of caution, we believe it appropriate to alert the court and the defence counsel to the issue. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: 90(d) has actually excluded only expert witnesses. Those are the only witnesses excluded from being out of court and out of hearing during the testimony of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. There is no discussion in here about the fact that there may be other witnesses, such as authentication witnesses, and I would also note, with respect to this, that not only do I believe that there is no reason that prosecution investigators would be under this Rule, in fact, the fact that they may have to do additional investigation, or analyse certain things means it is necessary that they be here, that, with respect to all the possible chain of custody or authentication documents, it is not even known now that they will be called. There are, I believe, approximately eight of them that we put down in our possible witness list, just in an excess of caution, in case there are issues that come up later. But I think the fact that it is not even now necessarily foreseen that they will have to be witnesses is another reason to allow them to be present, because otherwise it is possible that there would be none of the investigators who would be permitted to be present, and I believe that would be a severe hindrance to the efficient proceedings in this trial, as well as to any potential investigation work that needs to be done, either during this part of the case, or even during the defence case, in case the witnesses were needed in rebuttal. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Are you now prepared to strike them out of your list of witnesses to make them readily available to sit in here? Because as long as they remain in your list of witnesses, it would normally depend upon what you want them to say, for then to determine whether they would be fact witnesses or merely identifying documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, given, as far as we know, that they were not present during Celebici at all during 1992 I cannot imagine that they would be fact witnesses. In terms of whether or not we would be prepared to strike them, we would be prepared to strike them as long as everyone understands that, if the defence counsel later objects to certain documents, and then it becomes necessary for us to call one of the witnesses, we cannot anticipate exactly what the defence is going to raise with respect to chain of custody or authentication. At this point, none of the witnesses are on a definite list, but, in an effort to be totally forthcoming with the defence, we chose to be very inclusive as to our possible witness list. But, if it was necessary, we could take them off the list, but it would have to be with the idea that, if something unforeseen comes forward, we may have to call one of those with respect to chain of custody or authentication. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Because it seems to me the fears of the defence are still not allayed by your present suggestion. They are still having fears about the role these witnesses will be playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to our witness list, when we filed it we, in fact, filed why we might call the witnesses, and with respect to the prosecution investigators on the possible list, it says, with respect to all of them, if necessary on chain of custody issues, or explanations on how given evidence was obtained.
